books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

stimulus.text:
The table shows the share of eligible voters who cast ballots in presidential elections, 
from 1824 to 1840, as recorded by the U.S. Bureau of the Census.
| Year | Share of eligible voters who voted |
| 1824 | 26.9% |
| 1828 | 57.6% |
| 1832 | 55.4% |
| 1836 | 57.8% |
| 1840 | 80.2% |
stimulus.source_note: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note

parts.prompt: Briefly identify the trend in voter participation shown in the table.
parts.modelAnswer: Voter participation rose sharply, from 26.9 percent of eligible voters in 1824 to 80.2 percent in 1840. The biggest jump came between 1824 and 1828.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying the trend of sharply rising participation, with at least one correct figure from the table.
scoring.notEarned: Naming a single year with no trend does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE reason for the sharp rise in participation between 1824 and 1828.
parts.modelAnswer: Most states had dropped property qualifications for voting. Jackson's campaign against the “corrupt bargain” of 1824 then mobilized the new voters, so turnout more than doubled.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one reason for the rise, such as the fall of property qualifications, the larger electorate, or Jackson's mass campaign.
scoring.notEarned: Restating the numbers with no reason does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE limitation of the table as evidence about how democratic the United States had become.
parts.modelAnswer: The table counts only eligible voters, who were mostly free white men. High turnout says nothing about the women, enslaved people, and others who could not vote at all.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one limitation, such as counting only eligible voters, or the exclusion of women, enslaved people, and others from the electorate.
scoring.notEarned: Saying the table is limited without naming what it leaves out does not earn the point.
